source.title: Why Do We Need Weight Decay in Modern Deep Learning?
source.authors: Francesco D'Angelo; Maksym Andriushchenko; A. Varre; Nicolas Flammarion

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; figure values are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares weight decay settings and reports effects on test error for normally labeled data, bearing on part of V5. It does not test random-label fitting.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses random-label memorization only as cited prior work. Its own results compare weight-decay settings on ordinary training data; figure-only test-error values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The weight-decay ablations test V5's claim that explicit regularization is unnecessary for generalization on real data. The study does not test random-label memorization. Table 2 supplies numerical results omitted from the record.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's vision summary is accurate but incomplete. The authors attribute weight decay's benefits to enhanced SGD implicit regularization in multipass vision training, improved optimization in under-trained LLMs, and greater low-precision training stability. Their conclusion describes weight decay as seldom valuable as an explicit regularizer. They do not experimentally study random-label fitting.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies weight decay and learning rate on ordinary vision and language training tasks; it does not apply random labels or the original sources’ random-label intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test-error comparison depends on learning rate and weight decay; the authors emphasize their interaction.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight decay and large learning rates improve vision optimization dynamics; weight decay also improves LLM optimization and bfloat16 stability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight decay can benefit optimization and numerical stability independently of preventing memorization.

record.problems: The relevant vision test-error outcomes are shown in figures without recoverable numerical values in the supplied text. The study does not test random labels, and it reports limited computational scale.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise eligible result rows omitted. V5 was marked tested_not_extracted because its full statement also concerns random-label fitting, dropout, and augmentation, which this study does not test.

untested.parts: Training-time comparisons between real and random labels and convergence across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test error across random-label corruption fractions.
Fitting random labels despite regularization; dropout removal; controlled data-augmentation removal. Vision experiments omit augmentation but do not compare its presence versus absence.
Learning real patterns before memorizing noisy labels.

missing.what: Numerical CIFAR-10 test errors for snapshot ensembles and EMA across weight-decay and learning-rate settings, including zero-weight-decay controls. These permit assessing generalization without weight decay despite the unreadable figures.

Generalization gaps remain close to zero throughout training with weight decay 0, 0.1 and 0.3 for GPT-2 models with 124M and 774M parameters; validation loss for the 124M model depends on training loss rather than weight decay.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's blanket limits_scope verdict: better performance with weight decay and learning-rate dependence alone do not contradict V5's nonnecessity claim. Figure axis labels cannot substitute for curve values. Supporting verdicts above rely on omitted results in the supplied text.

relationships.condition: ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, snapshot ensembles and EMA, learning rates 0.1 and 0.15
relationships.reason: Missing Table 2 rows show 13% test error without weight decay for both averaging methods at both learning rates, versus best reported errors of 9% with weight decay. Useful generalization survives its removal; improvement with weight decay does not establish necessity.
relationships.display_finding: Both averaging methods yielded 13% test error without weight decay at both learning rates, versus best reported errors of 9% with it.

statements.correction: Appendix C.7, Table 2: at learning rates 0.1 and 0.15, snapshot ensembles and EMA each have test error 0.13 without weight decay and minimum error 0.09 with weight decay. At learning rate 0.05 and weight decay 0.0075, EMA error is 0.08. Appendix D, Figure 19: GPT-2 models with 124M and 774M parameters have near-zero generalization gaps throughout training, including without weight decay.
statements.problem: The 9% best-error comparison needs its learning-rate restriction: Table 2 also reports 8% EMA error. Near-zero GPT-2 generalization gaps are accurately reported but do not establish retained absolute held-out performance.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Vision experiments comparing weight decay settings
reader_labels.reason: The study reports that weight decay combined with a large learning rate improves test error, so the generalization outcome depends on the training setting (R1–R5); it does not establish that removing weight decay makes generalization poor.
